5 The Likelihood

5.1 Introduction and Definition

  • •

    The likelihood is a fundamental object in statistical inference. It plays a central role in both Frequentist and Bayesian approaches.

  • •

    We imagine we will gather data Xi, with i=1,…,n. Now, we may not know the precise distribution that generated the data, but we may suspect that the distribution is one of a family of possible distributions, labelled or parameterised by a parameter θ (in fact θ could even represent a list of parameters).

  • •

    We saw examples of this in Section 3 when we assumed the Xi had Bernoulli distribution with parameter p: here θ=p. Another example was seen in Section 4 when we sometimes assumed the Xi came from a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ2: here θ={μ,σ2}.

  • •

    The joint probability density function p.d.f. (or probability mass function p.m.f. if the Xi are discrete) of the data is simply represented as f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|θ), using the same notation we have used in Section 3.1.

  • •

    However, once we measure the data X1=x1,X2=x2,…,Xn=xn, the joint p.d.f. can now be viewed as just a function of θ, as the data are now fixed. This leads directly to the following definition.

Definition: The Likelihood function

Suppose X1,X2,…,Xn have a joint density f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|θ). Given an appropriate statistical model that provides a family of distributions parameterised by a fixed and unknown θ, the likelihood function, ℓ⁢(θ), is the joint density function, evaluated at the observed data, considered as a function of θ, i.e.

ℓ⁢(θ)≡ℓ⁢(θ;x1,x2,…,xn) =f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|θ),
and the log-likelihood function is its logarithm
ℒ⁢(θ)≡ℒ⁢(θ;x1,x2,…,xn) =log⁡ℓ⁢(θ)=log⁡f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|θ)

Definition: Likelihood for independent and identically distributed data.

Suppose each Xi has p.d.f. given by f⁢(x|θ), and that all the Xi are i.i.d., then we have that

ℓ⁢(θ)=f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|θ)= ∏i=1nf⁢(xi|θ)
and the log-likelihood function is given by
ℒ⁢(θ)=log⁡f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|θ)= log⁢∏i=1nf⁢(xi|θ)
= ∑i=1nlog⁡f⁢(xi|θ)

That is, the log likelihood is just the sum of all the individual log likelihoods. This is much easier to calculate with (and to maximise) as we shall see.

  • •

    Important! Note that ℓ⁢(θ) is a function of θ, but NOT a probability density function of θ. As a result, ℓ⁢(θ) needn’t share the behaviours of probability density functions, such as integrating to 1, etc.

  • •

    Additionally, from a frequentist point of view, θ is just a fixed but unknown parameter (so couldn’t have a probability distribution associated with it). In the Bayesian paradigm we can (and do) represent our beliefs about any quantities, including parameters such as θ, by a probability distribution. However, even this case, the likelihood still isn’t a probability distribution.

  • •

    However, ℓ⁢(θ) is extremely useful as it gives us a way of exploring which values of parameters θ were more likely to have generated the data we have seen.

  • •

    We have already seen its use in Section 3.2.5 for the case of Bernoulli trials.

Example: Likelihood for Bernoulli Trials

In the case of n Bernoulli trials (see Section 3.2.5) the i.i.d. Xi were each Bernoulli distributed with parameter p, that is Xi∼B⁢e⁢r⁢n⁢o⁢u⁢l⁢l⁢i⁢(p). In other words, the Xi are discrete and can only equal 0 or 1 with probabilities q=1−p and p respectively.

Hence we wrote the individual p.m.f. for each Xi as

f⁢(xi|p)={pxi⁢q1−xifor⁢xi=0,1,0otherwise. (70)

Now we can write down the likelihood as before, noting that our parameter of interest is now θ=p, so we use ℓ⁢(p) in place of the general ℓ⁢(θ):

ℓ⁢(p)=f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p) = ∏i=1nf⁢(xi|p) (71)
= ∏i=1npxi⁢q1−xi (72)
= p∑i=1nxi⁢q∑i=1n(1−xi) (73)
= px⁢qn−x (74)

where we again notice that the likelihood depends on the data only through the total number of observed successes, defined as x=∑i=1nxi.

The log likelihood, which in this case we just evaluate directly, we saw was:

ℒ⁢(p) = log⁡f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|p)=log⁡(px⁢qn−x) (75)
= x⁢log⁡p+(n−x)⁢log⁡(1−p) (76)

We then maximised this to find an estimator for p (more of this shortly!)

Example: Likelihood for the Binomial Scenario

In a Binomial scenario we have that X is the sum or count of the successes from n Bernoulli trials with parameter p, and therefore that X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p). When viewed in this framework, we just have one single experiment, that yields the realisation X=x. Hence, given realised data X=x, the likelihood ℓ⁢(p), which you actually calculated previously in tutorials, was given by

ℓ⁢(p)=f⁢(x|p)=(nx)⁢px⁢qn−x

and the log likelihood

ℒ⁢(p) = log⁡f⁢(x|p) (77)
= log⁡[(nx)⁢px⁢qn−x] (78)
= log⁡[n!(n−x)!⁢x!]+x⁢log⁡p+(n−x)⁢log⁡(1−p) (79)

Note the similarity between the likelihoods for the Bernoulli trials and the Binomial scenario.

  • •

    This is all fine, but what about a distribution that we haven’t used before?

  • •

    The Poisson distribution is often used to model radioactive decay counts and a wide range of other phenomena (traffic, queueing etc.).

  • •

    What is the likelihood of a sample of size n in this case?

Example: Likelihood for the Poisson Distribution

  • •

    If the distribution the data is drawn from is Poisson, then we say Xi∼P⁢o⁢(λ), where λ is the parameter of interest (it actually equals the expected number of counts, so E⁢[Xi]=λ).

  • •

    Let’s remind ourselves what the Poisson distribution looks like:

    f⁢(x|λ)=e−λ⁢λxx!for⁢x=0,1,2,… (80)
  • •

    Hence, if we have i.i.d. data Xi, with i=1,…,n, we can immediately find the likelihood with θ=λ:

    ℓ⁢(λ)=f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|λ) = ∏i=1nf⁢(xi|λ)
    = ∏i=1ne−λ⁢λxixi!
    = e−n⁢λ⁢λ(∑i=1nxi)∏i=1nxi!
  • •

    And therefore the log likelihood equals

    ℒ⁢(λ) = log⁡f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|λ)=log⁡[e−n⁢λ⁢λ∑i=1nxi∏i=1nxi!] (81)
    = −n⁢λ+(∑i=1nxi)⁢log⁡λ−log⁡(∏i=1nxi!) (82)
  • •

    Notice that this likelihood expression depends on the data only through the sum ∑i=1nxi and factorial product ∏i=1nxi! of the observed data. Crucially, however, notice that only the sum affects how the likelihood changes as λ varies…

5.2 Maximum Likelihood Estimation

  • •

    Again, this is all fine, but why do we care about this likelihood object?

  • •

    We care because it gives us (among other things) a very general procedure to estimate unknown parameters.

  • •

    This procedure is known as Maximum Likelihood Estimation: we just find the value of θ that maximises the likelihood for the given sample x1,…,xn.

  • •

    We typically denote this Maximum Likelihood Estimate as θ^MLE.

Definition: Maximum Likelihood Estimate θ^MLE

More formally, we define the Maximum Likelihood Estimate θ^MLE as

θ^MLE=arg⁡max𝜃⁢ℓ⁢(θ)=arg⁡max𝜃⁢ℒ⁢(θ) (83)

Note that, critically, the value of θ that maximises ℓ⁢(θ) is the same that maximises ℒ⁢(θ), due to the monotonicity of the log function, and hence we can instead just maximise ℒ⁢(θ), which is much easier!

  • •

    We can find θ^MLE in a large number of situations, hence it is a very general technique.

  • •

    In general, Maximum Likelihood Estimators have good properties, especially for large n, but note that they are not always unbiased.

Example: Maximum Likelihood Estimate for Bernoulli Trials

  • •

    We calculated this previously in Section 3.2.5. We had the log likelihood as

    ℒ⁢(p)=x⁢log⁡p+(n−x)⁢log⁡(1−p) (84)
  • •

    and found the value of p which we now denote as p^MLE, that satisfied

    ∂ℒ⁢(p)∂p = xp−(n−x)(1−p)=  0 (85)
    ⇔p^MLE = xn (86)
  • •

    Note that to ensure it is indeed a maximum we should also check the second derivative is negative:

    ∂2ℒ⁢(p)∂p2=−xp2−(n−x)(1−p)2<  0 (87)

Example: Maximum Likelihood Estimate for Binomial Scenario

  • •

    The MLE for the Binomial scenario is of course the same, as you saw in tutorials. We have the log-likelihood:

    ℒ⁢(p)=log⁡[n!(n−x)!⁢x!]+x⁢log⁡p+(n−x)⁢log⁡(1−p) (88)

    and now when we partially differentiate with respect to p, the first log⁡(nx) term disappears, and we recover the same expression as seen in the Bernoulli case:

    ∂ℒ⁢(p)∂p = xp−(n−x)(1−p)=  0 (89)
    ⇔p^MLE = xn (90)
  • •

    We know this is a maximum from before (so no need to check the second derivative again).

  • •

    We have already checked that this estimator p^MLE=p^=Y (viewed for general unmeasured data) is unbiased as E⁢[p^MLE]=p.

Example: Maximum Likelihood Estimate for Poisson Scenario

  • •

    For the case of i.i.d. Poisson data where Xi∼P⁢o⁢(λ) we had log-likelihood

    ℒ⁢(λ)=−n⁢λ+(∑i=1nxi)⁢log⁡λ−log⁡(∏i=1nxi!) (91)
  • •

    To find the Maximum Likelihood Estimate for λ here, which we denote as λ^MLE, we again partially differentiate, noting the thankful disappearance of the rather messy log⁡(∏i=1nxi!) term as it does not depend on λ:

    ∂ℒ⁢(λ)∂λ = −n+(∑i=1nxi)⁢1λ= 0 (92)
    ⇔λ^MLE = 1n⁢∑i=1nxi=x¯ (93)

    the sample mean.

  • •

    Before the data is measured we can view the general MLE as

    λ^MLE=1n⁢∑i=1nXi=X¯ (94)

    in which case we see that

    E⁢[λ^MLE]=E⁢[1n⁢∑i=1nXi]=1n⁢∑i=1nE⁢[Xi]=1n⁢∑i=1nλ=1n⁢n⁢λ=λ (95)

    and hence that, in this case the estimator λ^MLE is unbiased.

  • •

    We now have a very powerful method of constructing (typically well behaved) estimators for a wide variety of cases.

5.3 Sufficiency

  • •

    The structure of the Likelihood, and how it relates to the results of a Maximum Likelihood Estimate calculation, provides significant insight.

  • •

    We saw how additive terms in the log-likelihood (or equivalently, multiplicative terms in the likelihood) that were just composed of values of the data xi and which did not involve the parameter of interest θ, were essentially irrelevant when it came to calculating θ^MLE.

  • •

    This leads directly to the very deep concept of Sufficiency.

  • •

    Sufficient Statistics are simply functions (i.e. summaries) of the data such that, were we to know them, the remaining details of the data contain no additional information about θ. Quite a strong statement!

Definition: Sufficiency via the Factorisation Theorem

If we have a sample of data x1,…,xn, a statistic T⁢(x1,…,xn) is said to be sufficient for θ if and only if we can factorise the likelihood ℓ⁢(θ) in the following form:

ℓ⁢(θ)=f⁢(x1,…,xn|θ)=g⁢(T,θ)⁢h⁢(x1,…,xn) (96)

where we see that all the θ behaviour of the likelihood is tied together with T through the function g⁢(T,θ), but the extra behaviour of h⁢(x1,…,xn), that contains additional details of the data, is essentially irrelevant.

  • •

    Therefore, a sufficient statistic T contains all of the information about the parameter θ that we can extract from the sample x1,…,xn.

  • •

    Note that the above definition generalises to the case where T represents a vector of sufficient statistics.

  • •

    We see that if T is a sufficient statistic for θ, and if we then partially differentiate the likelihood we have that:

    ∂ℓ⁢(θ)∂θ=∂∂θ⁢[g⁢(T,θ)⁢h⁢(x1,…,xn)]=h⁢(x1,…,xn)⁢∂∂θ⁢g⁢(T,θ) (97)

    so that the MLE θ^M⁢L⁢E satisfies:

    h⁢(x1,…,xn)⁢∂∂θ⁢g⁢(T,θ^M⁢L⁢E)⇔∂∂θ⁢g⁢(T,θ^M⁢L⁢E)=  0. (98)

    (using h⁢(x1,…,xn)≠0 for any realised sample). Therefore, the MLE θ^MLE will only be a function of T, and not of any other components of the data x1,…,xn.

Example: Sufficiency for Bernoulli Trials

  • •

    For the Bernoulli trials we had likelihood

    ℓ⁢(p) =f⁢(x1,…,xn|p)=px⁢(1−p)n−x
    which can be written in the form of the Factorisation Theorem as
    ℓ⁢(p) =g⁢(x,p)⁢h⁢(x1,…,xn)
    withg⁢(x,p)=px⁢(1−p)n−xandh⁢(x1,…,xn)=  1
  • •

    Hence here T=x is the sufficient statistic for our parameter of interest θ=p (assuming as usual that n is fixed and known).

Example: Sufficiency for Binomial Scenario

  • •

    For the closely related Binomial Scenario we had likelihood

    ℓ⁢(p) =f⁢(x|p)=(nx)⁢px⁢(1−p)n−x
    which can be written in the form of the Factorisation Theorem as
    ℓ⁢(p) =g⁢(x,p)⁢h⁢(x)
    withg⁢(x,p)=px⁢(1−p)n−xandh⁢(x)=(nx)
  • •

    Hence the sufficient statistic is now the single data point T=x for our parameter of interest θ=p as before, again assuming we know n.

  • •

    Note that the concept of sufficiency gives deeper insight into the similarity between the Binomial scenario and the Bernoulli trials.

  • •

    We see that the Binomial distribution f⁢(x|p) is in fact the direct distribution of the sufficient statistic T=x for the Bernoulli trials. As a result, the Binomial analysis must return the same maximum likelihood estimate.

  • •

    We also see that there is no further simplification to the Bernoulli trials that one could make: any further simplification (e.g. rounding x to the nearest even number) would lose information, according to the likelihood. This type of concept is extremely important in today’s world of “big data”.

Example: Sufficiency for Poisson Data

  • •

    For the Poisson Scenario we had likelihood ℓ⁢(λ) in terms of the parameter λ:

    ℓ⁢(λ) =f⁢(x1,x2,…,xn|λ)=e−n⁢λ⁢λ(∑i=1nxi)∏i=1nxi!
    =e−n⁢λ⁢λn⁢x¯∏i=1nxi!
    where we have used n⁢x¯=∑i=1nxi. We can rewrite ℓ⁢(λ) in the form of the Factorisation Theorem as:
    ℓ⁢(λ) =g⁢(x¯,λ)⁢h⁢(x1,…,xn)
    withg⁢(x¯,λ)=e−n⁢λ⁢λn⁢x¯andh⁢(x1,…,xn)=1∏i=1nxi!
  • •

    Now we have T=x¯ is the sufficient statistic for our parameter of interest θ=λ, again assuming we know n.

  • •

    We also see that all the detailed dependence on the data in the h⁢(x1,…,xn) function can be discarded.

  • •

    Note that our choice of sufficient statistic was not unique: we could have used T=∑i=1nxi here instead of T=x¯.
